title: Ezekiel 16:23–34
context: The LORD continues the charge with a woe. Jerusalem built shrines on every street and sought alliances with the surrounding powers: Egypt, Assyria, and Chaldea (Babylon). In the allegory, these political alliances are pictured as unfaithfulness, because trusting foreign powers meant turning from the LORD. The LORD says he already reduced her portion and handed her over to the Philistines, who were ashamed of her conduct. Yet she was never satisfied. The section ends with a striking reversal: unlike others in such a trade, Jerusalem paid her lovers rather than being paid. These notes keep the imagery sober and focus on its meaning.

verses.text: “ ‘ “It has happened after all your wickedness—woe, woe to you!” says the Lord GOD—
verses.arminianNotes: “It has happened after all your wickedness—woe, woe to you!” Arminian readers hear the LORD's lament and warning interrupting the account, a cry that still invites the hearer to turn.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the woe is spoken by “the Lord GOD.” It marks a new stage of the indictment. Both traditions hear grief as well as judgment in the double woe.

verses.text: “that you have built for yourselves a vaulted place, and have made yourselves a lofty place in every street.
verses.arminianNotes: “that you have built for yourselves a vaulted place.” Arminian readers see shrines set up “in every street,” showing that idolatry had spread throughout public life.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the exact nature of the “vaulted place” and “lofty place” is uncertain. The point is clear: worship of other gods had become visible everywhere.

verses.text: You have built your lofty place at the head of every way, and have made your beauty an abomination, and have opened your feet to everyone who passed by, and multiplied your prostitution.
verses.arminianNotes: “You have built your lofty place at the head of every way.” Arminian readers see the city's beauty, given by the LORD, turned into “an abomination” through widespread unfaithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the allegory's language is deliberately shocking to expose the seriousness of idolatry. These notes keep to its meaning rather than its imagery.

verses.text: You have also committed sexual immorality with the Egyptians, your neighbors, great of flesh; and have multiplied your prostitution, to provoke me to anger.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD charges Jerusalem with unfaithfulness toward Egypt, her neighbors. Arminian readers see alliances with Egypt pictured as unfaithfulness, because they replaced trust in the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that political dependence on Egypt is a frequent target of the prophets. The allegory treats such alliances as provoking the LORD “to anger,” since they rival covenant loyalty.

verses.text: See therefore, I have stretched out my hand over you, and have diminished your portion, and delivered you to the will of those who hate you, the daughters of the Philistines, who are ashamed of your lewd way.
verses.arminianNotes: “See therefore, I have stretched out my hand over you.” Arminian readers see earlier discipline: the LORD “diminished your portion” and handed Jerusalem over to her enemies, as a warning meant to turn her back.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the irony that “the daughters of the Philistines” were ashamed of her conduct. Even pagan neighbors were shocked. The text does not name the specific event in view.

verses.text: You have played the prostitute also with the Assyrians, because you were insatiable; yes, you have played the prostitute with them, and yet you weren’t satisfied.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD charges Jerusalem with the same unfaithfulness toward Assyria. Arminian readers see alliances with Assyria in the same light: Jerusalem looked for security among the nations and “weren’t satisfied.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the repeated phrase about being unsatisfied shows the emptiness of trusting anything other than the LORD. Both traditions treat this as shared ground.

verses.text: You have moreover multiplied your prostitution to the land of merchants, to Chaldea; and yet you weren’t satisfied with this.
verses.arminianNotes: “to the land of merchants, to Chaldea.” Arminian readers see Babylon added to the list of nations Jerusalem turned to, and still she “weren’t satisfied with this.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the irony that Babylon, the power Jerusalem courted, became the instrument of her judgment, as the later chapters of Ezekiel show.

verses.text: “ ‘ “How weak is your heart,” says the Lord GOD, “since you do all these things, the work of an impudent prostitute;
verses.arminianNotes: “How weak is your heart,” says the Lord GOD. Arminian readers see the LORD diagnosing the inner cause: a heart without steadfastness, easily drawn away from him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in “How weak is your heart” a statement of the human heart's condition apart from grace. They connect it with the promise of a new heart in Ezekiel 36:26, pointing to the Deuteronomy 10:16 box rather than adding one here.

verses.text: in that you build your vaulted place at the head of every way, and make your lofty place in every street, and have not been as a prostitute, in that you scorn pay.
verses.arminianNotes: “in that you build your vaulted place at the head of every way.” Arminian readers see the LORD repeating the charge of verses 24–25 and adding that she “scorn pay,” introducing the reversal of verses 32–34.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the repetition emphasizes how widespread and persistent the idolatry had become. The next verses explain what makes Jerusalem's case unusual.

verses.text: “ ‘ “Adulterous wife, who takes strangers instead of her husband!
verses.arminianNotes: “Adulterous wife, who takes strangers instead of her husband!” Arminian readers see the core of the charge: covenant betrayal of the LORD, who is pictured as husband.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers compare Jeremiah 31:32, where the LORD says of the covenant, “which covenant of mine they broke, although I was a husband to them.” The marriage picture describes covenant loyalty.

verses.text: People give gifts to all prostitutes; but you give your gifts to all your lovers, and bribe them, that they may come to you on every side for your prostitution.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the shocking reversal: Jerusalem gave her gifts to her lovers and bribed them, spending what the LORD had given her.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the reversal exposes the folly of idolatry and foreign alliances. Jerusalem paid for what could not help her, which both traditions see as a sober warning.

verses.text: You are different from other women in your prostitution, in that no one follows you to play the prostitute; and whereas you give hire, and no hire is given to you, therefore you are different.” ’
verses.arminianNotes: “You are different from other women.” Arminian readers see the LORD summarizing the reversal: Jerusalem paid her partners rather than being paid, so her unfaithfulness cost her rather than profited her.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the section ends by stressing how unnatural Jerusalem's conduct was. The emphasis falls on the futility and ingratitude of turning from the LORD.
